articles.title: Wife 'felt stranger's hand' during sex, Philip Young trial told
articles.summary: Four men are currently on trial accused of sexual offences against Joanne Young, which they deny.
articles.body:
A woman said she locked herself in a bathroom after realising her then-husband had allowed someone else in the bedroom while she was blindfolded and having sex, a jury has heard.

In a police interview played at Winchester Crown Court, Joanne Young said she was restrained when she felt a hand on her wrist which she believed did not belong to her now ex-husband Philip Young.

Joanne - who has waived her legal right to anonymity - said Young, who has admitted drugging and raping her, later apologised and told her he had invited someone to watch the couple have sex after browsing online forums.

Warning: This story contains distressing details

On the second day of the four men's trial, two police interviews with Joanne were played to the court.

During the first interview, dated 29 July 2024, Joanne said the incident when she hid in the bathroom had happened in February 2023 after a night out with friends.

She told police she could not "remember all of it", but said Young had come upstairs after she had gone to bed.

Joanne said she "woke up with a blindfold and restraints on" and loosened the restraint on her right hand and then the left. At that point, she said, she felt a hand grip her wrist.

She said Young - who she believed was at the end of the bed - said "get down" to someone as she tried to take her blindfold off.

Joanne said she then saw someone ducking at the end of the bed and she ran to the bathroom and locked the door.

"The bed is a really big bed. So to have someone on the end of the bed and the left was not possible… I knew immediately," she told police.

The jury heard the couple discussed the incident, with Joanne telling police it was the first time she had ever seen her then-husband cry.

Joanne said she asked Young if he had ever invited anyone to watch them have sex before, which he denied.

"It was so intrusive. I was so upset. He knows I would have never said yes to that," she told police.

Joanne told the officer: "I didn't know if I should stay in the relationship or get myself out of the situation."

She said she took the incident as a "one-off" and tried to "move on".

Asked by an officer if there was a discussion between Young and Joanne about having someone else in the relationship, she said: "There was a joke years ago, a bit of banter, where he said in the kitchen something like 'would you ever want to sleep with someone else?'.

"I said no, and he said 'as long as I can watch you'. We laughed it off but it was a no."

She added: "It was never a part of our relationship. There'd never been a discussion. He never asked me what I wanted, it wasn't a conversation."

On the day Young was arrested, Joanne said he admitted to her he had shared images of her online without her consent.

Joanne said it had felt like a "kick in the stomach" and she was left in "shock and utter confusion".

She said: "How he could do that to me. How he could do something that's so intimate that's not allowed. How can he do it? How can you do that and think that was OK?"

The prosecution also read out statements from people who had been friends with Joanne and Young during their marriage.

Joanne's friend Susan said she thought the couple had a "dream relationship" before Joanne told her about the alleged incident of February 2023.

"She was in a real dark place about what happened," the statement said.

"After telling me, life went back to normal but what I witnessed from Jo was she didn't seem herself and that Phil had crossed a line from what he had done.

"Jo explained she was torn about why would Phil do this to her. She was in shock and seemed to be numb."

Emma Brown, who the court was told had been best friends with the couple since 2009, said Young "could handle his drink" and she "never saw him noticeably drunk".

"He was always on his mobile phone... I didn't know what he was doing as I didn't look at it," she added.

The four men jointly charged with Young, 50, are accused of the following offences:

Connor Sanderson-Doyle, of Swindon, denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching

Norman Macksoni, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape

Richard Wilkins, of Toothill, Swindon, Wiltshire, denies one count of rape and one of assault by penetration

Mohammed Hassan, of Swindon, denies one count of sexual touching

Jurors were shown videos earlier which allegedly showed Sanderson-Doyle, Wilkins and Macksoni sexually assaulting Joanne.

Young, a former Conservative Swindon councillor, previously admitted 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing an obscene article.

He also published more than 500 intimate images and videos of his ex-wife and recorded her doing private acts for his own sexual gratification without her consent between 2010 and 2024.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.

Young and Hamilton will be sentenced at the end of the trial, which is expected to last up to four weeks.

articles.title: Hundreds of World War I munitions exposed by melting ice removed from Dolomites
articles.summary: Some 250 World War I-era munitions that emerged from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Italian Dolomites have been removed.
articles.body: Some 250 World War I-era munitions that emerged from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Italian Dolomites have been removed. Artillery shells, mortar bombs and other ammunition had initially been found in the Trentino-Alto Adige region by hikers, naturalists and, in one case, after a road accident, according to a statement sent to CNN Tuesday by the Italian army’s Julia Alpine brigade. The first unexploded ordinance found this summer was a 90-millimeter mortar shell discovered in June after a car rolled down a ravine near Caldonazzo after the driver forgot to engage the hand brake when parking the vehicle, the army said. When firefighters removed the vehicle, they noticed the shell dating back to World War I at the foot of a tree. It was later removed by a specialized bomb squad. The other devices, which were from the White War fought between Italian and Austro-Hungarian armies between 1915 and 1918, were concentrated in an area popular with hikers during the summer and had been covered in snow and ice for more than 100 years. Specialists from the 2nd Engineer Regiment of the Julia Alpine brigade, who specialize in high-risk high-altitude rescue and military operations, began the clean-up in early August, a spokesperson from the unit told CNN Tuesday. The summer reclamation campaign ended on October 16. The ordinances were found on trails frequently traversed by climbers, hikers and mountain workers, as well as areas inaccessible to the public. The army said the campaign to clear the munitions required “solid mountaineering skills” to navigate “inaccessible areas, at high altitudes, and on particularly challenging terrain.” In the area between the Cima del Frate mountain peak and Forcella Fierollo mountain pass near the hamlet Bieno, a cache of 75-millimeter artillery shells caused the closure of a popular mountaineering route during the removal earlier this month. The route was later reopened. Munitions from both World War I and II are revealed each year, but specialized work can only take place in the late summer and early fall when weather conditions allow for safer operations before snow begins in late October, the army said. The extreme heat over the last few years has led to the fast retreat of the Caré Alto and the Lares glaciers, which make the area less stable for workers. A safety campaign is underway to warn hikers and local mountain dwellers not to touch or move suspicious munitions if found. Instead, they should be reported to local authorities, ideally with accompanying photos. Low winter snowfall in 2025 and extreme temperatures in the summer of 2026 have accelerated the melting of the glaciers in the Trentino region, according to local authorities.

articles.body: These five people are making the world a better place with their kindness, compassion, and courage. They are the Top 5 CNN Heroes of 2026, a group of everyday people who saw problems and found unique ways to help solve them. They were all nominated by you – our audience – and selected by CNN to each receive a $10,000 prize. And starting today, you can vote at CNN.com/Heroes to help decide who will be the next CNN Hero of the Year and receive an additional $100,000 to continue their inspiring work. The Top 5 CNN Heroes will receive a grant along with organizational and capacity-building support from The Elevate Prize Foundation, a global nonprofit on a mission to Make Good Famous, committed to bringing visibility to the work of changemakers and inspiring the world. CNN has once again teamed up with Pledge, the award-winning fundraising platform trusted by millions, to power giving for this year’s Heroes. Supporters can learn more and donate directly to the Top 5 CNN Heroes’ nonprofits from CNN.com/Heroes. To find out who is named Hero of the Year, watch the 20th annual CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute, hosted by Anderson Cooper and Laura Coates, airing on Saturday, December 5, at 8 p.m. ET. Here’s a look at this year’s Top 5 CNN Heroes: Dion Dawson: Dion’s Chicago Dream Growing up on Chicago’s South Side, he endured homelessness and food insecurity – often waiting for hours in line at food pantries. Since 2020, the US Navy veteran has made it his mission to fight food insecurity in his hometown with a new approach. His nonprofit, Dion’s Chicago Dream, employs dozens of community members who deliver more than 80,000 pounds of free, fresh produce to thousands of households every week all over the city – helping recipients live healthier, less stressful lives. “We’re the Dream Team. It’s about giving your community the best possible chance to succeed.” Read Dion’s full story Dr. Gladys Kalema-Zikusoka: Conservation Through Public Health As Uganda’s first wildlife veterinarian, Dr. Gladys Kalema-Zikusoka has devoted her life to protecting the endangered mountain gorillas in Bwindi Impenetrable National Park. When she realized their survival was intertwined with the conditions in local communities, she founded her nonprofit, Conservation Through Public Health. Since 2003, her organization’s health and economic initiatives have educated and empowered more than 10,000 households, and the area’s gorilla population has grown by more than 50 percent. “I always get very excited when I hear that a baby mountain gorilla has been born. As long as the communities see the gorillas as their future, the numbers are going to keep growing.” Read Gladys’ full story Andrew Lunetta: A Tiny Home for Good While volunteering at homeless shelters, Andrew Lunetta quickly learned that people weren’t failing at housing; housing was failing them. That insight led him to start A Tiny Home for Good, which helps people experiencing homelessness rebuild their lives with stability, dignity, and ongoing support. Based in Syracuse, New York, the organization has built 23 tiny homes and refurbished more than a dozen others, housing 47 tenants in permanent, supportive homes paired with long-term case management. “For my tenants, I want a sense of stability and I want connection. If our tenants are afforded both those things, then I’m doing my job.” Read Andrew’s full story Jaina Spagis: Cats of San Bernardino Caring for a stray cat and its kittens in her backyard opened her eyes to the overwhelming number of community cats in need in Southern California. The experience sparked her mission to provide a lifeline for street cats and co-found her nonprofit, Cats of San Bernardino. Today, her organization leads trap-neuter-return efforts; feeds established colonies; rescues and provides medical care for high-need cats; and has placed roughly 2,000 cats and kittens into homes. “They give me a sense of purpose. I see cats like I see people. They all have different personalities. They all have worth.” Read Jaina’s full story Kiko Trujillo: Arizona Sonora Border Projects for Inclusion An industrial engineer, Francisco ‘Kiko’ Trujillo saw first-hand the barriers facing people with disabilities in poverty-stricken areas along the US-Mexico border. Born and raised in Nogales, Mexico, he co-founded Arizona Sonora Border Projects for Inclusion, known as ARSOBO. The group empowers low-income families through custom wheelchairs, prosthetics, hearing devices, and rehabilitation programs while also employing disabled individuals. To date, ARSOBO has served nearly 3,500 people with disabilities. “We are changing the lives of not just the patient, but the entire family.” Read Kiko’s full story

articles.title: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his position on the EU
articles.summary: The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the Brexit deal at a summit in Brussels next month.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.

The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.

He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.

Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.

"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.

"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.

"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.

"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."

Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.

It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.

Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .

Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.

"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."

Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.

"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.

At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.

articles.title: Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi meets Ahmed al-Sharaa in historic Syria visit
articles.summary: Talks focused on enhancing trade, reviving Baniyas oil pipeline and achieving stability through cooperation.
articles.body:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has arrived in Damascus to meet with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on the first visit of an Iraqi prime minister to Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad.

The visit comes as the two neighbours seek to strengthen bilateral ties and boost economic and oil cooperation.

According to the official Iraqi News Agency (INA), the two leaders discussed the export of Iraqi oil through the Baniyas line , increasing the volume of trade exchange and joint work to develop the agricultural sector to achieve food and economic integration.

Iraq has recently begun exporting limited quantities of oil through Syria following the outbreak of the US-led war on Iran.

Last July, the two countries signed agreements to revive the Haditha Baniyas pipeline to transport Iraqi oil in addition to signing a memorandum of understanding with a consortium of three companies, most notably the American oil major Chevron to implement the project.

“The Iraqi and Syrian people are one people in two countries,” Zaidi said according to INA, noting that “work to develop partnership and joint cooperation in various fields especially economic and social affairs, enhance security co-operation, unify positions on regional and international issues, and work to achieve peace and stability in the region”.

For his part, the Syrian president expressed his “great appreciation for the visit of al-Zaidi and his accompanying delegation,” stressing “the depth of bilateral relations and Syria’s keenness to achieve the highest levels of cooperation between the two countries”.

Al-Sharaa and al-Zaidi had previously met last September in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, where they discussed ways to strengthen political and security coordination and expand economic and trade cooperation.

articles.title: Dutch zookeeper dies after being attacked by leopard
articles.summary: A zookeeper has died from her injuries days after she was attacked by a leopard at the Dutch safari park where she worked.
articles.body: A zookeeper has died from her injuries days after she was attacked by a leopard at the Dutch safari park where she worked. The unnamed employee, who had worked at the Beekse Bergen safari park for almost four decades, was attacked by the animal on Saturday and died on Tuesday. “With enormous sadness, we have to report that the animal caretaker of safari park Beekse Bergen passed away today from the injuries she sustained on Saturday, October 24, in an incident with a leopard in the park,” the park said in a statement Tuesday. “Her passing also deeply affects us all, and we are intensely grieving with her family, friends and loved ones. We ask for peace and privacy for her loved ones and our staff, so that they can process this profound loss,” the statement added. The woman suffered serious wounds to her head and neck while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards, the Associated Press reported. The woman contacted colleagues via a walkie talkie after the incident in the leopard’s enclosure and an ambulance and trauma helicopter were dispatched at around 11 a.m. local time Saturday, AP added. She underwent emergency surgery but her condition worsened on Sunday evening. The employee joined the park, located in the southern Netherlands, when she was 17 years old and had worked there “with short breaks for almost 40 years,” the park’s statement added. CNN affiliate NOS reported that the zookeeper had been working with the leopards for eight years and had been working alone in the enclosure with two male Persian leopards when she was attacked. There are no cameras inside the enclosure, the park told NOS, which also reported that the animals have been treated as normal since the incident. The park said that an independent investigation had been launched into the woman’s death. Home to more than 100 species of animals, Beekse Bergen offers visitors the choice of seeing the safari park by foot, car, bus and boat. This is not the first time a member of staff at a zoo or safari park has been fatally injured by an animal. In 2023, a zookeeper was killed in Austria after being attacked by a rhino. The incident, in which another zookeeper was injured, occurred at Salzburg Hellbrunn Zoo. Two years prior to that, a woman working at a safari park in Chile was killed by a tiger while working in the big cats’ enclosure. CNN’s Rose Roobeek contributed to this report.

articles.title: Why are three of the UK’s four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea?
articles.summary: The deployment marks the first time in years that three Vanguard-class vessels have been at sea at the same time.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has simultaneously deployed three of its four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea for the first time in five years, The Times reported on Wednesday.

At least one of the vessels – known as Vanguard-class submarines – was said to be armed with ballistic missiles which carry nuclear warheads.

The report named the three submarines at sea as HMS Vanguard, HMS Vigilant and HMS Vengeance, with the fourth, HMS Victorious, currently undergoing maintenance.

A navy source quoted by The Times described the deployment as “unusual”, without elaborating.

The UK continuously deploys at least one of the four submarines as a security guarantee.

The deployment has raised questions over whether the UK has changed its defence posture after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned last week that Britain should be prepared for war.

The last time three submarines were at sea was more than five years ago, according to The Times.

Navy Lookout, the UK’s leading independent publication on the Royal Navy, says one submarine carrying ballistic missiles has been at sea without interruption since 1969.

It said the second vessel was believed to be preparing to relieve a patrol boat, while the third was likely conducting sea trials or work-up activity.

Last year HMS Vanguard patrolled the seas for 200 days, just a week shy of the longest known submarine deployment of 207 days, carried out by HMS Victorious in 2021.

According to Sky News, a spokesperson for the defence ministry said the country’s nuclear deterrent is the “cornerstone of our national security, protecting the UK and our NATO allies every moment of every day”.

“We remain the only European ally to commit its nuclear deterrent to the defence of NATO. This means that all NATO allies already benefit from the protection of our nuclear deterrent,” the spokesperson added.

Last week, British and French fighter jets flew together in their first joint exercise involving France’s airborne nuclear capability.

The French armed forces ministry said British RAF Typhoon fighters escorted the French jets, simulating a nuclear strike.

France’s Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said that having “independent nuclear forces does not preclude coordination”.

“Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom continues to deepen,” she added.

The UK’s Streeting said that in an “increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt”.

“The United Kingdom and France stand together in their commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations,” he added.

What are the UK’s ‘war readiness’ plans?

On Saturday, Streeting wrote in the Telegraph newspaper that Britain must be ready for war within 1,000 days.

“Our adversaries’ willingness to harm us is not new. What has changed is their capacity. By 2030, their force strength and war economy could put them in a position to attack,” Streeting wrote.

“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win. This Government will make sure it is mission accomplished,” he said.

His message followed last week’s launch of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign, which called on households to store three days’ supply of tinned food and water bottles, cash and a wind-up radio in case of a cyberattack or a weather event which disrupts infrastructure.

The warning also followed reports that Russia has been using fishing trawlers to track and spy on the UK’s undersea cables.

articles.title: Meet Ian Smith, the 81-year-old British former dentist who started posting TikTok videos to promote his novel and attracted 1.5 million followers with life advice
articles.summary: At 81, Ian Smith from Snettisham in Norfolk, England, has attracted a large following on TikTok by sharing short videos about positivity, motivation and
articles.body: At 81, Ian Smith from Snettisham in Norfolk, England, has attracted a large following on TikTok by sharing short videos about positivity, motivation and lessons from life. The former dentist retired in 2022 after decades in the profession, and his social media journey began with a different ambition: promoting a self-published novel after hundreds of literary agents he approached sent back only 3 responses. According to a BBC report published on April 18, 2026, Smith was then posting 2 videos a day and had 1.5 million followers. His most-viewed clip had reportedly crossed 59 million views. The figures reflect the time of that report, rather than a verified count today. His online journey began with a book, but his videos eventually took a different direction.Ian Smith’s TikTok journey began with a self-published novelSmith first turned to social media to find readers for a novel he had written himself. After approaching hundreds of literary agents and receiving just 3 responses, he decided to self-publish the book and promote it online, including through BookTok, the TikTok community devoted to books and reading. His wife encouraged him to start posting videos and challenged him to reach even 100 followers. Smith took the remark as motivation and continued creating content. According to the BBC, he had been posting regularly for around 18 months by April 2026, but his videos had shifted towards messages of motivation and positivity. The change in subject matter gave his account a broader focus than book promotion. Instead of concentrating solely on his novel, Smith began sharing thoughts and advice drawn from his experiences, attracting viewers from different parts of the world.Why an 81-year-old TikTok creator has attracted younger viewersThe BBC reported in April 2026 that people in their 20s made up the largest age bracket among Smith’s followers. His audience also included viewers from countries such as Brazil, illustrating the international reach described in the report. Smith told the BBC that the response to his videos was both “staggering” and “humbling”. He described the experience of speaking into a small phone and receiving responses from people around the world. He also said he had not received negative comments. The BBC’s account documented the scale of Smith’s audience at the time, but it did not establish a single reason for his popularity. His videos centre on encouragement and positivity, while his own account of the experience highlights the unexpected connections he has made through posting online.What research says about social connection and purpose in later lifeResearch offers context for some of the themes associated with Smith’s videos, although it cannot establish why individual viewers follow him or whether his social media activity has improved his health. A 2010 meta-analysis published in PLOS Medicine, titled “Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review”, examined 148 studies involving 308,849 participants. The researchers found that stronger social relationships were associated with a 50% greater likelihood of survival compared with weaker social relationships. The findings concerned social relationships broadly and should not be interpreted as proof that online engagement alone produces the same benefits.A separate study published in JAMA Network Open in 2019, titled “Association Between Life Purpose and Mortality Among US Adults Older Than 50 Years”, analysed data from 6,985 adults older than 50. It found an association between a stronger sense of purpose in life and lower all-cause mortality. The observational findings do not prove that purpose directly causes longer life, but they add to research examining how psychological and social factors relate to health in later adulthood. Another study, “Longevity Increased by Positive Self-Perceptions of Aging”, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 2002, followed 660 participants aged 50 and older. It found that more positive self-perceptions of ageing were associated with longer survival, with the relationship corresponding to a 7.5-year difference in lifespan after adjustment for other factors.These studies examine different aspects of social relationships, purpose and perceptions of ageing. None specifically investigates TikTok creators or establishes a health effect from posting videos. Smith’s experience is an individual example of someone who found a new audience through social media after retirement, rather than evidence that online popularity necessarily improves wellbeing. His story began as an attempt to find readers for a novel.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Espionage threats blur lines between security and dissent in Iran
articles.summary: Iran is using the threat of spy networks to detain and execute political opponents, analysts say.
articles.body:
While two wars on Iran by the United States and Israel have exposed serious vulnerabilities in Iran’s intelligence and security institutions, Iran is using the threat to crack down on dissent, analysts have said.

Saeid Golkar, an associate professor in political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, said the genuine espionage threats faced by Iran were illustrated by the killing of high-level figures, including former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the latest assault by Israel and the US on February 28.

“At the same time, the regime has historically used real or, most of the time, perceived security threats to justify political repression and expand its coercive apparatus,” Golkar told Al Jazeera.

“The current crackdown appears to reflect both legitimate counterintelligence concerns and the regime’s broader efforts to suppress dissent and intimidate society.”

Former Israeli spy chief David Barnea recently said that in the weeks before Israel launched its 12-day war on Iran in June 2025, he had approved the entry into the country of dozens of agents with clear intelligence or sabotage assignments.

“I can’t say that they are here with us. But they are there in Tehran, living their lives,” he told a conference in Israel on October 22.

According to Barnea, who was the director of Mossad for five years until June 2026, Israeli intelligence tried to maximise the number of Iranian citizens arrested by local authorities in order to shield its genuine agents inside Iran.

Just hours after launching the war and killing senior commanders and nuclear scientists, they deliberately released footage of agents inside Iran with a Mossad logo, leading to the arrests of thousands of people with no links to the Israeli intelligence service.

Barnea claimed the strategy worked, and almost all of their assets remained unidentified. Eight months into a second war launched by Israel and the US against Iran, with the stated aim of overthrowing the Islamic republic, Iran’s paranoia remains.

Iranian authorities have significantly accelerated judicial punishments for cases linked to national security since the 2025 war. That has entailed mass arrests, expedited prosecutions, lengthy imprisonment, asset confiscations and executions.

The people targeted include alleged spies but also protesters, journalists, lawyers and minorities. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have documented cases involving coerced confessions, the denial of effective defence and national security charges applied to dissenters.

“The espionage threat facing Iran is very real. The two US-Israeli wars exposed serious vulnerabilities in Iran’s intelligence and security apparatus… Tehran has legitimate concerns about foreign infiltration, sabotage, and intelligence operations inside the country, especially as the threat of another military escalation remains high,” Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said.

“But there is a fundamental distinction between espionage and dissent,” she added. “Espionage involves covertly gathering sensitive intelligence or assisting foreign intelligence operations. Criticising the government, reporting on its failures, engaging with foreign media, or challenging official narratives does not, in itself, constitute espionage. The Iranian authorities have increasingly blurred this distinction, treating political opposition and independent reporting as extensions of foreign intelligence activity.”

Iranian authorities argue that foreign intelligence operations are aimed not only at overthrowing the government but also fragmenting the country.

Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence said in May that “enemies” were combining espionage, sabotage, hostile media, exploitation of economic crises and fuelling ethnic and sectarian tensions as part of a “hybrid war”.

Judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei has repeatedly invoked wartime conditions and domestic laws to argue for urgent security measures, and accelerated the punishment of alleged collaborators as a means of protecting the country.

Judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said earlier in October that there were active cases involving at least 1,895 people, including 94 media workers, accused of cooperation with Israel or other hostile states. Police had announced at least 21,000 arrests following the June 2025 war, while at least 50,000 people were detained in connection with the nationwide protests in January 2026. Thousands of civilians were killed in the crackdown against antigovernment protests across Iran, according to US-based rights organisation HRANA.

The authorities have referred to the nationwide protests as a “coup” orchestrated entirely by Israeli and US intelligence agencies. The Iranian government also claims that Mossad and other intelligence agents killed protesters. But an independent United Nations fact-finding mission said the authorities committed crimes against humanity during their most violent crackdown since the revolution.

Executions linked with security charges have also increased following the wars and protests. At least 19 people were hanged in espionage-related cases between June and December 2025, according to the UN.

Iran Human Rights, an Oslo-based nonprofit group, said it recorded 16 espionage defendants executed between January and September 2026, alongside 33 protesters and 13 prisoners affiliated with banned groups. The group had tracked at least 604 executions by early October.

Amnesty International reported at least 34 executions this year linked to the January nationwide protests by October 13, including five between September 30 and October 5.

Iranian authorities have warned the public about Mossad and other intelligence agencies running cyber-operations to expand their influence in Iran, accusing them of recruiting people through social media and online offers.

Sending images or information to networks deemed to be hostile to the Iranian government – including BBC Persian – could result in sentences of 10 to 15 years in prison and heavy fines. Combined with other offences, it could lead to potential charges of “corruption on Earth”, which carry the death penalty.

The authorities also regard the Starlink satellite internet service as a “tool of war” used for espionage, information gathering and even operating drones by “enemy” agents inside Iran. Tens of thousands of Starlink terminals have been smuggled into the country despite severe punishments for distributing and using the service. Iranian authorities have tried to confiscate or jam them.

For several days during the 12-day war, 20 days during the January protests and 88 days at the start of the current war, Iran imposed a near-total internet shutdown on 90 million Iranians. The official reasons ranged from protecting national assets against cyberattacks to disrupting hostile drones. The global internet remains severely filtered in Iran, and authorities have warned it could be disrupted again in case of military escalation.

University of Tennessee at Chattanooga’s Golkar said that by blurring the line between espionage and political opposition, authorities increasingly treat protesters, journalists and ordinary citizens as potential threats to national security.

“Ultimately, the Islamic republic increasingly treats regime security and national security as interchangeable concepts. While counterespionage is a legitimate state function, it has also become a tool to protect the ruling establishment and expand the influence of security institutions,” he said.

“In brief, and over time, the Islamic republic has transformed into a security-dominated regime that increasingly securitises nearly every aspect of political and social life, including peaceful civic activism, treating even nonviolent expressions of dissent as potential threats to regime survival”.

articles.title: US moves closer to PERM overhaul amid crackdown on green card sponsorship
articles.summary: The Trump administration is moving closer to overhauling the employment-based green card sponsorship process, even as major technology companies face
articles.body: The Trump administration is moving closer to overhauling the employment-based green card sponsorship process, even as major technology companies face scrutiny over recruitment practices.The US department of labour’s (DOL) proposed rule to modernise the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme cleared review by the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs on Oct 23. Publication in the Federal Register will follow shortly, and public comments will be invited. DOL will then consider the feedback before finalisation of the rule, a process that could take months.The proposal, titled Modernising the Labour Market Test and Improving Protections for US Workers in the PERM Immigrant Visa Program, could significantly change how employers recruit US workers before sponsoring foreign nationals for permanent residence.H-1B visas generally allow foreign professionals to work in the US for up to six years. For those seeking a green card through their employer, PERM is often a critical first step. Employers must conduct prescribed recruitment to establish that no able, willing, qualified and available US workers can fill the position, and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans. Once PERM is certified, the employer can generally proceed to the next stage by filing an immigrant application. The regulations have not undergone a comprehensive overhaul since 2004.According to DOL’s regulatory agenda, the proposed rule aims to modernise recruitment standards, strengthen safeguards for US workers affected by layoffs, improve compliance with non-discrimination requirements and revisit record-retention obligations.Immigration attorneys expect greater scrutiny of recruitment practices and documentation. An in-house counsel at a multinational company said the changes could significantly affect recruitment planning and layoff-related safeguards.“For instance, if layoffs have been for a now redundant process and hiring is for emerging AI technology, this would need to be documented and proved,” the counsel explained.The regulatory initiative comes amid an enforcement crackdown on employers sponsoring foreign workers. In a significant case, California-based data management company Cloudera agreed to a two-year PERM debarment following allegations that it deliberately excluded American applicants from technology jobs.According to the US department of justice, Cloudera created a separate recruitment process for seven positions earmarked for workers holding temporary visas. US applicants were allegedly directed to submit resumes to an email address that could not receive external messages. Under a settlement announced recently, Cloudera agreed to establish a $1.4 million back-pay fund for affected workers and pay $600,000 in civil penalties. It also faces monitoring and compliance obligations.Following an earlier suspension of Cloudera’s PERM processing, the wider crackdown reportedly extended to eight other major employers: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.Separately, DOL is pursuing revisions to prevailing wage rules affecting H-1B and PERM sponsorship, potentially increasing employers’ costs.You use AI every day. articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after losing Brazil’s presidential election
articles.summary: Bolsonaro and his family fled to the US amid a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.
articles.body:
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and his family have landed in Miami, Florida, after the candidate lost Sunday’s presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva .

Al Jazeera’s John Holman, reporting from outside Opa Locka Executive Airport, where the family landed on Wednesday morning, said the group was “whisked away in an SUV” from the airport soon after arriving.

Dressed casually in a dark polo shirt and flanked by his wife and two daughters, Bolsonaro stepped out of the plane shortly after it landed in Miami at around 9:30am local time (1:30pm GMT). Florida is home to the largest population of Brazilians in the U.S.

Brazil ‘s Supreme Court had ordered Flavio Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports shortly after the election, in an attempt to make sure the right-wing senator did not flee the country before he could be investigated for embezzlement and money laundering.

As a senator, Bolsonaro had immunity from potential criminal prosecution, but he would lose that protection in January, since he gave up his seat to run for president.

Holman said the Bolsonaro family’s flight from Brazil was a dramatic escape, starting with crossing into neighboring Argentina “on a row bridge, by foot.”

Argentine immigration authorities said Flavio and his family entered the country late Tuesday night, and less than an hour later boarded a private plane operated by Baires Fly destined for Guayaquil, Ecuador.

That plane arrived in Ecuador, and later took off for Miami, Florida, with Flavio and his family on board.

Both Ecuador and Argentina are run by right-wing leaders who are close allies of United States President Donald Trump, said Holman. The countries provided “stepping stones among allies.” The US State Department has issued visas for the family.

Brazil and the US do have an extradition treaty, but Holman said it is expected Bolsonaro will be protected by Trump, who said yesterday the Bolsonaros were “fine people.”

“The signs are, with the State Department issuing him a visa, with the comments coming from President Trump, that they’re not gonna be in any hurry to hand him back to Brazil,” Holman said.

Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, undertook a very similar journey to Florida after he lost his bid for reelection in 2022. While he was in the US, the elder Bolsonaro’s supporters attempted to orchestrate a coup attempt. He later returned to Brazil, and is currently under house arrest.

articles.title: Are GCC countries looking for a regional security pact with Iran?
articles.summary: Observers say diverging views are unlikely to turn current diplomatic efforts into a lasting infrastructure.
articles.body:
Gulf countries have stepped up diplomacy with Iran in a bid to de-escalate tensions across the Middle East, amid fears of renewed US strikes on Tehran and intensifying hostilities between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

The three nations that signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August – Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye – and diplomats from Qatar met with high-ranking Iranian officials on Monday in an effort to prevent the resumption of all-out war.

Underscoring the high stakes, the meeting in Tehran was attended by Saudi Minister of Defence Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, just days after Iran-aligned Houthi fighters struck Saudi airports , ports and oil facilities.

Meanwhile, during a diplomatic visit to the United Kingdom’s University of Cambridge on Monday, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called for a regional security framework, including a “non-aggression pact”, between the Gulf countries and Iran under which the United States would no longer be the primary provider of security.

While Gulf countries appear determined to avoid another round of conflict – which has already restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupted global oil and gas supplies and wreaked havoc on energy facilities and infrastructure in Gulf states – questions remain over whether a regional agreement is possible and where it would leave relations between the US and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).

On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated warnings that Washington may carry out another military operation against Iran as rising fuel prices weigh on the US midterm elections scheduled for November 3. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Iran would respond more forcefully to any renewed US military action, stoking fears of an even wider escalation.

While this week’s talks in Tehran mark the first high-level ‌contact between Iran and the Mecca mutual defence pact nations since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, reports suggest they have stopped short of landing an agreement.

Reuters reported that Qatari mediators ⁠presented ⁠Iran with a draft deal on Sunday, which Tehran was expected to respond to by the end of the week. On Wednesday, the news agency quoted Iranian officials as saying Qatar had put ‌forward ideas that were unacceptable and that Tehran would ⁠show ⁠no flexibility regarding the nuclear ‌issue.

Khaled Batarfi, a Saudi political analyst and academic, said the visit to Tehran indicated that Saudi Arabia was willing to give Iran a “last warning” and “submit to the region’s concerns”, but that Iran has so far refused.

“The gap is [wide] and what makes it worse is that there is no trust,” Batarfi told Al Jazeera.

Observers say diverging views are unlikely to turn the current diplomatic efforts into a lasting infrastructure. “It’s really hard to see a regional security framework coming out in the coming months or even years,” Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, an associate fellow at Chatham House in London, told Al Jazeera.

“What we are seeing is more small groups, flexible groups of countries that are taking the lead in trying to reach either bilateral or multilateral solutions,” the analyst said. “A regional security framework would need the same vision for the region, which is not necessarily shared… among the GCC countries themselves.”

Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye share concerns that a prolonged confrontation between Iran and the US could further destabilise the region.

“The main obstacle remains the fundamental disagreement between Tehran and Washington over the sequence of commitments,” Azizi told Al Jazeera. “The US wants Iranian concessions, particularly on the nuclear issue, while Tehran insists that its conditions for ending the war must be met first.”

“Regional mediation could help bridge this gap, possibly through an interim arrangement, but the willingness of regional actors to facilitate an agreement does not necessarily mean that the two principal parties are prepared to make the necessary compromises,” he added.

As for a new security order, Azizi said regional countries do not share a common understanding of what it should look like and what role the US – which has so far been the GCC’s main security partner – would have left to play.

Iran has long advocated for a regional security architecture that would reduce or eliminate the US military presence. “Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, however, remain deeply integrated into the US security system, and there is little indication that they intend to abandon it,” Azizi said.

“The recent war has certainly raised questions about the reliability of American security guarantees, but this has encouraged these countries to diversify their security partnerships rather than fundamentally redefine their strategic alignments.”

articles.title: Holocaust educator says Mamdani could learn from UK's targeted approach to antisemitism in schools
articles.summary: Britain accepted all 27 school antisemitism recommendations, drawing a sharp contrast with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's broader plan.
articles.body: The British government’s decision to embrace sweeping measures addressing antisemitism in schools is drawing a sharp contrast with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s recently unveiled strategy, raising questions about why Britain’s plan appears more specific than the one proposed in America’s most Jewish city. The U.K. government accepted all 27 recommendations from an independent review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England. The measures include encouraging adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism, specialized training for educators, strengthened reporting procedures and independent oversight. Mamdani’s 33-page strategy — while not only focused on education — by comparison, does not adopt a single definition of antisemitism, explicitly address the relationship between anti-Zionism and antisemitism or establish numerical benchmarks for measuring whether its initiatives succeed. British Jewish author and Holocaust educator Dov Forman, who recently graduated from university, said Mamdani could learn from Britain’s targeted approach to addressing antisemitism in schools. MAMDANI PLEDGES MILLIONS TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM WHILE LEAVING KEY QUESTION UNRESOLVED The British review followed a BBC report from Yavneh College, a Jewish secondary school near London, where students described how antisemitism has affected their daily lives. Their accounts offered a window into the urgency behind the government’s recommendations. Education provides one of the clearest points of comparison between the two strategies. Mamdani's plan calls for expanding Holocaust education, including opportunities for students to visit the Museum of Jewish Heritage, while also addressing how public schools respond to antisemitic discrimination. The U.K. government's recommendations address many of those same concerns, placing greater emphasis on how educators recognize antisemitism, how schools respond when incidents occur and what protections are in place for Jewish students. The review, led by former senior education official Sir David Bell, found that nearly three in five Jewish people between the ages of 16 and 19 had experienced or witnessed antisemitism. It concluded that antisemitism is a distinct form of racism requiring a specific response and called for clearer guidance to distinguish legitimate political debate from harassment, intimidation and antisemitic rhetoric. British Jewish author and Holocaust educator Dov Forman, who recently graduated from university, called the recommendations "the bare minimum," while acknowledging that the government is attempting to confront the problem directly. "The least [Mamdani] could do is look at what has happened in the U.K. and adopt similar measures, such as adopting the IHRA definition, which is the agreed definition across the world and where there is a consensus of what antisemitism actually is," Forman told Fox News Digital. "The basic way to solve antisemitism is to actually agree on what it is and to understand that targeting a Jew deliberately because of what is going on in Israel, for example, is antisemitic, as the IHRA definition says," he added. Forman cautioned that the British recommendations remain largely optional and that their effectiveness will depend on whether institutions act. "I do think some of them will be enforced and listened to. I do worry, though, that the government says things and does not actually take it seriously enough." Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government would establish an implementation group, while Bell was commissioned to conduct an independent assessment of its progress after one year. Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun, the U.S. special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism, welcomed Britain’s decision while emphasizing that adopting recommendations is only the beginning. JEWISH EDUCATORS FACE RAMPANT ANTISEMITISM IN TEACHERS UNIONS, NEW REPORT FINDS "I welcome the U.K.’s announcement that it has accepted all 27 recommendations," Kaploun wrote on X. "Now, the challenge lies in implementation and enforcement." Forman also said that British officials must examine whether their rhetoric about Israel contradicts their stated commitment to protecting Jewish communities. "It is very rich of the government to say that schools should adopt the IHRA definition of antisemitism and that Jews should not be demonized for what is going on in the Middle East, and then for them to get up in the dispatch box in the House of Commons every week and blame Israel," he said. "Stop talking and start acting," Forman added, calling on the government to confront Islamist extremism and the Muslim Brotherhood and identify more directly where antisemitism is originating. The U.K. has faced criticism for being slow in combating antisemitism. Jewish residents have faced physical attacks, threats and harassment, making the specificity of its new plan and its contrast with New York City’s approach particularly notable. Rabbi Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, called Mamdani’s strategy a "paper tiger," arguing that its announced $36 million price tag obscures how little would go directly toward physical security. "It’s a million dollars in security in a city with a million Jews. It’s a dollar a Jew," Steinmetz told Fox News Digital. The strategy includes $1 million to support physical security for vulnerable nonprofit organizations, including synagogues and other houses of worship, and $6.4 million for grants through the city’s Partners Against the Hate initiative. Steinmetz claimed that much of the money would support cultural centers and broadly defined community initiatives rather than immediate security needs. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER UJA-Federation of New York, the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York, the American Jewish Committee’s New York office and the New York Board of Rabbis issued a joint statement warning that Mamdani’s plan fails to address a central source of contemporary antisemitism. The organizations said rhetoric demonizing or delegitimizing Israel contributes to Jewish New Yorkers being treated as suspect, excluded or unsafe, and argued that any serious strategy must acknowledge that connection. "How can you have a strategy to keep New York Jews safe when you can’t even name what the danger is?" Steinmetz asked. One of Mamdani’s early actions as mayor was to revoke an executive order issued by former Mayor Eric Adams adopting the IHRA definition for city agencies. The definition provides examples of when criticism of Israel may cross into antisemitism while making clear that criticism comparable to that directed at any other country is not inherently antisemitic. Fox News Digital asked Mamdani’s office why the city’s strategy omits the IHRA definition and measurable benchmarks, and whether the administration would consider safeguards similar to those adopted by Britain. The mayor’s office did not respond by the time of publication. Britain’s measures have also only recently been accepted, and their impact remains untested. articles.title: More Goole council homes to be fitted with solar panels
articles.summary: The project in Goole is part of a council scheme to help tenants reduce energy costs.
articles.body:
More than 300 more council homes in the Goole area are to be fitted with solar panels in a bid to cut tenants' energy bills and reduce carbon emissions.

As part of an investment programme by East Riding of Yorkshire Council during the 2026-27 financial year, solar panels, energy-efficient LED lighting and improved loft insulation will be installed.

Once the work is completed, around March 2027, more than 400 council homes in the town will have solar panels, almost a third of the council-owned properties in the area.

The solar panels will also allow tenants to use renewable electricity generated at their home, with surplus electricity able to be exported to the National Grid.

Michael Lee, council cabinet member for housing and infrastructure, said: "We're proud to invest in our council housing stock, to create warmer and more energy-efficient homes that help both tenants and the environment."

articles.title: Dolores Huerta, farmworker and civil rights activist, dies at 96
articles.summary: Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers with César Chávez, improving the lives of the country's mostly Latino farmworkers and changing the course of the labor movement.
articles.body: Dolores Huerta, arguably the nation's most well-known Latina civil-rights leader, has passed away at 96, her family said in a statement. The labor leader and civil rights activist was the co-founder, with Cesar Chavez, of the United Farm Workers (UFW), the first nationally recognized union for farm workers. An inspiration to generations of Americans, Huerta spent decades fighting labor injustices and political, racial and gender inequality. Huerta was “the most famous Latina that has ever been in the labor movement, and the renown was well-earned,” said Matthew J. Garcia, professor at Dartmouth College and author of the 2014 book, “From the Jaws of Victory: The Triumph and Tragedy of Cesar Chavez and the Farm Worker Movement.” “She was extraordinary.” In her UFW heyday, Huerta cut a striking figure, a fierce young Latina shouting through a bullhorn, rallying workers and leading marches. This was a rare sight at a time when Hispanics had yet to become a political force. She was the embodiment of a “Chicana,” a politically active Mexican American woman claiming her own power. Though she was most famous for her leadership in the United Farm Workers, Huerta was committed to social and political activism throughout her life, supporting voting rights, immigrant rights, environmental justice, LGBTQ+ equality and other issues. She was arrested more than 25 times for participating in non-violent civil disobedience activities. In 2019, at 89, she was arrested while joining a union protest for better pay for home health care workers. She also prominently campaigned for many Democratic candidates. In 1993 Huerta was the first Latina inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame. In 2012, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. In a shocking coda to her life story, Huerta revealed in 2026 that Chavez had sexually abused her during their time as union leaders. This revelation came as part of a bombshell investigation by the New York Times, alleging that Chavez had groomed and abused girls and women. Huerta had not known about the young girls’ and young women’s allegations, she said. In a statement about her revelations, Huerta said, “I carried this secret for as long as I did because building the movement and securing farmworker rights was my life’s work.” Of Mexican American descent, Huerta was born in 1930 in New Mexico and grew up in Stockton, California. Civic engagement was part of her family tradition. “My father was an assemblyman; I had a cousin who was a judge. When we were kids, we used to listen to FDR’s fireside chats,” she said. “When I turned 21, part of my birthday ritual was to go and register to vote.” After college, Huerta worked as a teacher. But she was shocked to see the children of farm workers coming to school barefoot and hungry, and living in homes with dirt floors. Determined to make more of a difference in people’s lives, she decided to become a community organizer. In her mid–20s, Huerta joined a California Latino civil rights group as a lobbyist, working in Sacramento in support of pensions for noncitizens and disability insurance for farm workers. Then came a turning point in Huerta’s life, when she met fellow organizer Cesar Chavez at a 1955 fundraising dinner. They shared an interest in the welfare of farm workers, and seven years later they launched the National Farm Workers Association, a forerunner to the UFW. Although Chavez was the face of the movement, Huerta’s organizing was essential to its success in winning farm workers the right to collectively bargain for better wages and working conditions. It was she who coined the slogan “Sí se puede” (Yes we can!), which became the rallying cry of the farm worker movement. Through protests, strikes, and grassroots campaigns, the UFW helped improve the lives of some of the country’s poorest and most marginalized workers. From the mid-60s to the mid-70s, millions of Americans participated in boycotts of grapes and lettuce. It was a heady time, Huerta recalled in the 2017 documentary about her life, “Dolores.” “We had this ambience all around you, that you could really change the world," she said in the documentary. It was during this time that Huerta experienced two separate unwanted sexual encounters with Chavez. The first time, Huerta told the Times, was in 1960, when Chavez pressured her into sex. The second time was in 1966, a situation that Huerta described as rape. These traumatic experiences became a dark secret that she would keep for nearly 60 years, even as she became a much-admired feminist and labor icon. “Dolores was by Cesar Chavez’ side the whole way through,” said Garcia. “They took what had been a largely rural movement and turned it into a cause that captured the national imagination.” Huerta, he pointed out, brought the UFW’s message into places like Los Angeles and New York City. “She was also a tenacious and strong negotiator of contracts on behalf of farm workers.” Despite Huerta’s significant efforts with the UFW, her role was often overlooked. “She was as strong a figure as Cesar was... I think she is an unsung hero in many parts of the U.S., and in our history,” said Domingo Garcia, former national president of the League of United Latin American Citizens. “Dolores stood for courage. She stood for righteousness and justice when it was unpopular to do so — and when there could be consequences for doing so.” Huerta helped mobilize working-class and poor people, Garcia said, “but she never backed down. She is a profile in courage that every American should know about, especially Latinos and women.” In speaking her truth about the abuse she suffered, in 2026 Huerta was hailed by Latino civic and advocacy organizations for her courage. Yet Huerta’s legacy will always be intertwined with that of Chavez. “I have never identified myself as a victim, but I now understand that I am a survivor — of violence, of sexual abuse, of domineering men who saw me, and other women, as property, or things to control,” Huerta said in her 2026 statement. “My heart aches for everyone who suffered alone and in silence for years.” Huerta noted that the farm worker movement had always been bigger than one individual. “Cesar’s actions do not diminish the permanent improvements achieved for farmworkers with the help of thousands of people,” she said. “We must continue to engage and support our community, which needs advocacy and activism now more than ever.” In her mid–20s, Huerta joined a California Latino civil rights group as a lobbyist, working in Sacramento in support of pensions for noncitizens and disability insurance for farm workers. These early legislative victories were among Huerta’s proudest achievements. Huerta was “the most famous Latina that has ever been in the labor movement, and the renown was well-earned,” said Matthew J. Garcia, professor at Dartmouth College and author of the 2014 book, “From the Jaws of Victory: The Triumph and Tragedy of Cesar Chavez and the Farm Worker Movement.” “She was extraordinary.” In her UFW heyday, Huerta cut a striking figure, a fierce young Hispanic woman shouting through a bullhorn, rallying workers and leading marches. This was a rare sight at a time when Latinos had yet to become a political force. She was the embodiment of a “Chicana,” a politically active Mexican American woman claiming her own power. “Dolores was by Cesar Chavez’ side the whole way through,” said Garcia. “They took what had been a largely rural movement and turned it into a cause that captured the national imagination.” Huerta, he pointed out, brought the UFW’s message into places like Los Angeles and New York City. “She was also a tenacious and strong negotiator of contracts on behalf of farm workers.” Huerta’s involvement with the UFW came at great personal cost. The mother of 11 children, she left several children behind with relatives when she went to organize farmworkers in the fields. She was often not available for her other children due to the demands of her work. Despite Huerta’s significant efforts with the UFW, her role was often overlooked by the media and historians. “She was as strong a figure as Cesar was — I think she is an unsung hero in many parts of the U.S., and in our history,” said Domingo Garcia, national president of the League of United Latin American Citizens. “Dolores stood for courage. She stood for righteousness and justice when it was unpopular to do so — and when there could be consequences for doing so.” Huerta helped mobilize working-class and poor people, Garica said, “but she never backed down. She is a profile in courage that every American should know about, especially Latinos and women.” Within the UFW, Huerta saw gender-based inequality, which led to an awakening of her feminist identity. “When I went to Delano (California) to work with the farmworkers, I had to tamp down my feelings about women in power because there was a different ambiance with the male dominance in the movement. There were a lot of women in the movement, but we saw we needed to be on the executive board,” she reflected in 2017. “The feminists helped me understand why it was important for women to be able to have control of their bodies and control of their lives.” Huerta was arrested more than 25 times for participating in nonviolent civil disobedience activities and strikes, even late in life. In 1988, at age 58, Dolores was assaulted by a police officer while protesting the policies of then-presidential candidate George H.W. Bush in San Francisco. In 2019, at 89, she was arrested while joining a union protest for better pay for home health care workers. Huerta was committed to activism throughout her life, supporting voting rights, immigrant rights, LGBTQ+ equality and environmental justice. She founded the Dolores Huerta Foundation in 2003 to “create networks of healthy, organized communities pursuing social justice through systemic and structural transformation,” according to its website. Huerta married her first husband Ralph Head in 1948. They had two daughters together. Her second husband was Venturo Huerta, with whom she had five children. She had four children with her longtime partner Richard Chavez (brother of Cesar), who passed away in 2011. By 2024, Huerta was pleased by the progress that Latinos had made, in areas like political representation and education, but remained concerned about threats to democracy. “Fascism, and voter suppression, is real,” she said. “But my optimism comes from knowing that we, the people, have the power to change things; if we organize, if we vote, and when we elect representatives who will enact policies that benefit all people.” As the country’s political and social landscape changed during her lifetime, Huerta never waved in her belief that people united in common cause can alter their circumstances. “When people come together and take collective action,” she said in 2020,” whether it’s in a march, whether it’s in a union election or, most important, come together to vote, this is how we make change.” Among her many honors, in 1993 Huerta became the first Latina inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame. In 2012, then-President Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian award. Upon receiving this prestigious award, Huerta noted, “The great social justice changes in our country have happened when people came together, organized, and took direct action. It is this right that sustains and nurtures our democracy today.”

articles.title: Hell will freeze over before Havana gives in to Trump. But regular Cubans don’t have that long
articles.summary: After 60 years of US sanctions, Cuba’s communist leadership is waiting out Trump. Whether its people can hold out that long is another matter.
articles.body: Can Cuba outlast Trump? The US president has vowed that Cuba could be the next US adversary to face his wrath. “What we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran,” Trump said at campaign rally in Florida on Friday. “Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands.” In his second term, Trump has already ramped up economic sanctions on the communist-run island to an unprecedented level, cut off the supply of oil required to power its collapsing electrical grid, and threatened military action. But amid the saber rattling and pressure campaign, Cuba’s government has managed to hold on to power. Officials on the island say they won’t be strong-armed into accepting a deal — even as the island teeters on the verge of economic collapse, with growing disparities between Cuba’s haves and have nots. “Sometimes we are asked, how has Cuba resisted what we have resisted? How was Cuba able to resist during the summer with the perverse aims to destabilize the country?” said Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla at a news conference last week ahead of an annual General Assembly at the United Nations on the US economic embargo on Cuba. After enduring 60 years of US economic sanctions, Cuba’s communist leadership seems to believe they can afford to wait out Trump and whatever comes next. There is little sign that the Cuban government is considering making the wide-ranging concessions the US is demanding of Havana. The Trump administration says they will keep up the pressure until Havana opens the island’s political system and economy, allows Cuban exiles a greater ability to return and invest in their homeland, and ends their alliances with Russia, China and other US adversaries. Hell will freeze over first seems to be the response from Havana. “I am convinced that the policies of the US government have to change,” Rodríguez said, “With this government or the following or the one after that.” There has been little progress in the talks that have been held and on Tuesday, ahead of the vote at the UN, Rodríguez attempted to interrupt US Ambassador Mike Waltz from giving a speech blasting the Cuban government. “Back away, this isn’t Havana,” Waltz told Rodríguez from the UN podium as the Cuban diplomat approached him. Growing inequality Ironically, as Cubans face the worst crisis of their lives, a small group here have made overnight fortunes importing gasoline, food and other hard-to-find items, profiting off the growing desperation. For those with the right connections, finding loopholes around the US embargo on Cuba and the tightly controlled Cuban economy has been a booming business. It’s no longer uncommon to see women with children in their arms begging at stoplights as new Audis and Teslas drive by; an impossible-to-imagine sight just a few years ago. I was recently in a gourmet store in Havana that opened up for Cuba’s elites where pricey Wagyu steaks, Russian caviar and Spanish olive oil were for sale, when a disheveled Cuban man walked in through the electric sliding door. Glancing at a piece of frozen meat for sale at about 10 times the average monthly salary, the man turned to a hovering sales attendant. “That price can’t be right, can it?” he said. The Trump administration is hoping to take advantage of those glaring inequalities by recruiting disaffected officials within the Cuban government. “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a Cuban-American and longtime opponent to the Cuban government, posted on X on Friday. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA,” the post continued. Cuban officials quickly fired back at the open effort to recruit spies inside the island. “Now the USA is resorting to public recruitment ads. There must be a lot of desperation and poverty in the agency’s ranks when it has to sell its offerings like toothpaste,” Cuba’s top diplomat for US affairs Carlos Fernández de Cossío responded on X. How long can this go on for? The US has already spent decades and hundreds of millions of dollars trying to topple the Cuban government with little to show for those efforts. Cuban officials quietly say that if Trump continues to be bogged down with the war in Iran and suffers a defeat that changes the US political landscape in the mid-term elections, regime change in Cuba could slip down his list of priorities. ​​Any deal with the Cuban government is likely to face intense blowback from anti-communist Cuban exiles in Miami who believe that Fidel Castro’s revolution is drawing its last breath. But how long can regular Cubans hold out? The government has announced a series of reforms that so far seem to have done little to jump-start the floundering economy. Officials for the first time have said that Cubans can amass wealth as the island warily opens to more capitalism. But many Cubans complain only insiders with the right connections are able to cash in. On a recent morning, before the sun came up, a group of retired Cubans stood in a line outside a government-run bank three hours before the doors opened to try and collect their shrinking pensions. Several said they had been unable to receive their pension for several days as power kept going out in the neighborhood. Retired construction worker Armando Ruiz said he was waiting for his monthly pension of 3,900 pesos, less than five dollars at black market exchange rates as the Cuban peso’s value plummets. “It’s only enough to get a little bit to eat,” he told CNN. “Sometimes you say how long can this go on for?”
